transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Um… I guess what brought me in is that some of the things that usually keep me feeling like myself have started to feel kind of… flat. Not terrible, exactly, but heavier than they should.

I used to like going on photography walks, helping mentor the kids, even just keeping my calendar clean and organized. Lately I’ve sort of stopped starting those things, if that makes sense. I’m not trying to be lazy or anything—I just don’t seem to get myself going the way I normally do.
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things as much as you used to, or that activities you once looked forward to feel more like a chore?

Yeah… I think that’s fair to say. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, because I’m still managing things, but the stuff that usually helps me feel like me—going out for photography walks, mentoring the kids, even keeping my calendar neat—has started to feel kind of flat. Like heavier than it should.

I still know those things matter to me, but I’m not really starting them the way I used to. They feel more like something I have to push myself toward, if that makes sense.
How long have you been feeling this way?

It’s been… longer than I’d like to admit, I guess. Maybe about a year and three months.

It kind of started after a family member’s health and behavior changed, and I ended up taking on more of the coordinating and keeping-track-of-things. I don’t want to overstate it, but since then, this flat feeling has just sort of stayed around. Does that make sense?
Would you say that most days you feel down or sad, and if so, how long does that feeling usually last?

I’m not sure I’d call it “sad” most days, exactly. It’s more like… low or kind of dulled out. Some days it’s there in the background for a good chunk of the day, but I can still get through what I need to do.

I don’t know if that answers it the right way. It’s not like I’m crying all day or anything… just not as light as I used to feel.
Have you noticed that you feel fatigued or that you’ve lost your energy, even when you haven’t been doing much physically?

Yeah… I think so, though I’m not sure if I’d call it physical fatigue exactly. It’s more like I have to push harder to start things.

The reason I came in is that the things that usually make me feel like myself—my photography walks, mentoring the kids, even keeping my calendar clean—started feeling kind of flat and heavy. And I just… stopped initiating them the way I normally would.

I can still do things when I really need to, so I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but the energy to begin is definitely not there like it used to be. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Would you say that your mood has been consistently low or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

I don’t think I’d say “depressed most of the day nearly every day,” no. At least… that sounds stronger than what I’ve been feeling.

It’s more like it comes and goes, or sits in the background. Some days are heavier, but I can still function and be pleasant with people. I’m not sure if I’m answering that in the way you’re looking for, but I wouldn’t want to overstate it.

Can you tell me a bit more about how you’ve felt when you’ve tried to start those activities, like your photography walks or mentoring the kids—do they still feel meaningful or enjoyable to you, even if you have to push yourself to start them?

They do still matter to me, I think. I don’t want to make it sound like I suddenly don’t care about them at all. It’s more that when I think about starting—like getting my camera bag ready or reaching out about mentoring—it feels… heavier than it should.

Once I’m there, sometimes I can get into it a little, but the pull toward it isn’t the same. Those things used to feel like they gave me energy, like they were part of who I am. Lately they feel kind of flat, and I’ve just stopped being the person who initiates them.

I’m not sure if that’s enjoyment being gone, or motivation, or what you’d call it. Does that make sense?
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to focus, make decisions, or think clearly lately?

A little, yeah. I wouldn’t say I’m falling apart or anything—work is still getting done overall—but I’ve noticed I’m not as sharp with some of the details.

Like with calendars, I’ve missed a couple of things I normally wouldn’t miss, or I’ll catch myself having to double-check tasks that used to feel automatic. That bothers me, because being reliable is kind of… my thing.

And outside of work, I think part of why I’ve pulled back from the photography outings and mentoring is that I don’t feel as present as I should. I don’t want to show up halfway, if that makes sense. Does that answer what you mean?
Can you tell me if you’ve noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, even when you manage to start them?

Yes… I think so. I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, because it’s not like I hate those things now or anything.

But the things that usually make me feel like myself—photography walks, mentoring the kids, even keeping my calendar clean and organized—they’ve started feeling kind of flat. Heavy, maybe. And even when I do manage to start, it doesn’t quite give me the same feeling it used to.

Honestly, what made me come in is that I just stopped initiating them. I’d think about doing them, and then… I wouldn’t. That’s not really like me. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Would you say that you’ve completely lost interest in those activities, or is it more that you still care about them but just can’t seem to get yourself to do them?

I wouldn’t say I’ve completely lost interest, no. I still care about them, and I think that’s part of why it bothers me.

It’s more like… the things that usually make me feel like myself—going out with my camera, mentoring the kids, even just keeping my calendar clean—started feeling flat and heavy. And then I just stopped being the one to start them.

So I guess it’s not that they mean nothing to me. It’s more that I can’t seem to get myself to do them the way I used to. Does that make sense?
Would you say that when you do manage to start those activities, like the photography walks or mentoring, you get less pleasure or satisfaction out of them than you used to?

Yeah… I think it is less satisfying than it used to be. Not gone completely, I don’t want to overstate it, but it feels flatter.

Like, if I do go out with my camera, I can still recognize that it’s something I care about, but it doesn’t really lift me the same way. Same with mentoring—I’m glad it matters, but I don’t feel as engaged or energized by it.

What made me come in is that those things usually make me feel like myself, and lately they’ve felt kind of heavy, so I’ve stopped initiating them. I’m not sure if I’m explaining that right.
Have you noticed that your ability to get things done at work or at home has slowed down or become more difficult because of these feelings?

A little, yes. I mean, I’m still getting my work done overall—I don’t want to make it sound like everything’s falling apart.

But I have noticed I’m missing small calendar details, or I’ll have to double-check things that used to be automatic for me. That bothers me, because being on top of those things is kind of my job.

At home, or outside of work, it’s more that I’ve pulled back from the photography outings and mentoring. I don’t feel as present or reliable as I usually do, so I think I’ve avoided starting them. I’m not sure if that counts as impairment, but it has made things harder.
Would you say that your mood has been persistently low or down for most of the day, more days than not, over the past two weeks?

I’m not sure I’d say it’s been persistently low most of the day, exactly. I mean… I’ve had down stretches, sure, but I don’t want to label it bigger than it is.

It’s more like feeling kind of muted or weighed down at times, especially when I’m trying to get started on things. But “most of the day, more days than not” — I’d have to think about that. I don’t know if I can say yes to that cleanly.
Over the past two weeks, would you say that your mood has been down or low for most of the day, nearly every day?

I don’t think I can say nearly every day, no. I’ve definitely had moments where I feel down or kind of heavy, but “most of the day” feels stronger than what I’m noticing.

I don’t want to underreport it either, but… if you’re asking strictly, I’d say I’m not sure it reaches that level. Does that make sense?
Over the past two weeks, have you had days where your mood felt down or low for most of the day?

Maybe a few, yes… but I’m a little hesitant to say “most of the day,” because I don’t know that I’ve been tracking it that clearly.

There have been days where I felt lower or heavier for a good chunk of the day, but not like I was completely unable to function. I’m still doing what I need to do, mostly. So… yes, some days, but I’m not sure how strong to make that answer.
Have you felt like the things you used to care about don’t matter to you as much anymore, even when you’re doing them?

Yeah… I think that’s actually part of why I came in.

I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, because I still care about those things in my head, if that makes sense. But the stuff that usually makes me feel like me—going out for photography walks, mentoring the kids, even just keeping my calendar really clean and organized—it’s been feeling kind of flat. Heavier than it should.

And I’ve noticed I’m not really starting those things on my own the way I normally would. I can do them if I have to, but the pull toward them isn’t there as much. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Over the past two weeks, have you felt a loss of interest or pleasure in almost all activities, even the ones you used to enjoy the most?

Almost all activities… I don’t know if I’d say it that broadly, because I can still do things and I don’t want to overstate it.

But yes, the things that usually make me feel like myself have felt kind of flat. Like photography walks, mentoring the kids, even keeping my calendar clean and organized — normally those give me some satisfaction, and lately they just feel heavier. I’ve noticed I’m not really initiating them the way I usually would.

So… not “nothing matters,” exactly, but the interest or pleasure is definitely reduced. Is that a fair way to put it?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant loss of interest or pleasure in most activities, which would help distinguish between moderate and severe recurrent depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Over the past two weeks, have you felt a loss of interest or pleasure in almost all activities, even the ones you used to enjoy the most?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: What made me come in is that the things that usually make me feel like myself—photography walks, mentoring the kids, even keeping a clean calendar—started feeling flat and heavy, and I just stopped initiating them.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking about diminished interest or pleasure in activities, which matches the negative symptoms profile describing loss of motivation, emotional engagement, and reduced initiation of normally meaningful activities.

patient.answer:
Almost all activities… I don’t know if I’d say it that broadly, because I can still do things and I don’t want to overstate it.

But yes, the things that usually make me feel like myself have felt kind of flat. Like photography walks, mentoring the kids, even keeping my calendar clean and organized — normally those give me some satisfaction, and lately they just feel heavier. I’ve noticed I’m not really initiating them the way I usually would.

So… not “nothing matters,” exactly, but the interest or pleasure is definitely reduced. Is that a fair way to put it?

opening_question.intent: Greet the patient and open the interview by asking about their reason for seeking help today
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a persistent low mood, diminished interest or pleasure in previously enjoyed activities, reduced energy, and impaired concentration over a prolonged period (>2 years), consistent with persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia). The symptoms do not meet full criteria for a major depressive episode, and there is no history of manic or hypomanic episodes, ruling out more severe recurrent depressive disorder or bipolar disorder.
